title: Consumer Protection
summary: Consumer protection means safeguarding consumers against unfair trade practices and exploitation by producers, traders and service providers, and providing remedies when they are cheated. It is needed because of consumer ignorance, unorganised consumers, widespread exploitation, the huge variety of goods, misleading advertisements, and because services cannot be checked before buying. National Consumer Day is observed on 24 December (the day the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 was passed).

(1) Adulteration — mixing something inferior into the product (argemone in mustard oil, papaya seeds in black pepper, kerosene in petrol). (2) Sale of spurious products — fake goods sold as genuine, often medicines. (3) False weights and measures — goods weighed or measured short, sweets weighed with the box. (4) Sale of duplicates — goods carrying marks of superior quality or well-known brands that they are not. (5) Hoarding and black-marketing — holding back stocks to create artificial scarcity, then selling secretly above the fixed price. (6) Sale of sub-standard goods that do not meet prescribed safety standards. (7) Tie-in sales — forcing the purchase of another product with the one wanted. (8) Misleading advertisements — falsely claiming superior quality (an air purifier claiming to remove 100% germs). (9) Gifts and lotteries that are not genuine; poor after-sales service; overcharging above MRP.

Consumers — self-help is the best help: know and assert their rights, form associations. Businessmen — supply quality goods at fair prices, avoid malpractices, settle complaints, follow fair trade; trade associations and chambers of commerce act against members who cheat. Government — pass and enforce laws, set up consumer courts, include consumer representatives in policy bodies, run awareness campaigns (Jago Grahak Jago). Businesses cannot say nothing can be done, and the government is not indifferent.

Agricultural Products (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937 — grading and certification of agricultural products with the AGMARK seal. Industries (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 — control over production and distribution of manufactured goods. Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 — severe punishment for adulteration of food. Essential Commodities Act, 1955 — control of production, supply and price of essential goods; action against hoarders and black-marketers. Standards of Weights and Measures Act, 1956 (and 1976) — standard metric weights and measures. MRTP Act, 1969 — action against restrictive and unfair trade practices. Prevention of Black-marketing and Maintenance of Essential Supplies Act, 1980. Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 — BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) sets quality standards and certifies products with the ISI mark (electrical appliances); hallmark for jewellery. Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (COPRA) — the most comprehensive law: six consumer rights, three-tier consumer courts and cheap, quick redressal for goods and services; replaced by the Consumer Protection Act, 2019.

Under the 1986 Act (as in the NIOS book): District Forum — claims up to ₹20 lakh; State Commission — above ₹20 lakh up to ₹1 crore, and appeals against District Forums; National Commission (New Delhi) — above ₹1 crore, and appeals against State Commissions; appeals against the National Commission go to the Supreme Court. Under the 2019 Act as revised in 2021: District Commission up to ₹50 lakh; State Commission ₹50 lakh to ₹2 crore; National Commission above ₹2 crore. The Supreme Court is not a consumer court.

A consumer or a consumer association files a written complaint (with the cash memo and other documents) within two years of the cause of action, by post or in person, with a nominal fee. Cases are to be decided within three months, or five months if the product needs laboratory testing. Reliefs (directions to the opposite party): remove the defect or deficiency; replace the goods; refund the price; pay compensation for loss or injury; stop the unfair practice; withdraw hazardous goods; pay corrective advertising.

Voluntary, non-profit bodies such as the Consumer Guidance Society of India (Mumbai) and CERC (Ahmedabad). They educate consumers through seminars and workshops; give legal aid and file cases on their behalf; represent consumers on official bodies; test competing products comparatively and publish results; publish journals; and suggest new laws and policies to government.

or: State the jurisdiction of the District Commission under the Consumer Protection Act.
It hears complaints where the value of goods or services paid does not exceed the limit — ₹20 lakh under the 1986 Act; ₹1 crore under the 2019 Act, revised to ₹50 lakh in 2021 — within its district.

vsa: Briefly outline the purpose of the Agricultural Products (Grading and Marking) Act, 1937.
It provides for grading and certifying the quality of agricultural products. Products meeting the standards may carry the AGMARK seal, assuring consumers of quality and purity.
April 2026
Write two features of services that make consumer protection essential.

(1) Services cannot be seen or checked before they are bought, so consumers cannot judge their quality in advance.
(2) Services cannot be stored or returned — a bad service (transport, medical treatment) cannot be replaced.
October 2025
Describe the role of NGOs in protecting consumers.
NGOs educate consumers about their rights through seminars and journals, give legal aid and file cases for them, test products and publish results, and represent consumers on government bodies.
October 2025
Explain the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986.

It set up the Bureau of Indian Standards (in place of the ISI) to protect consumers. BIS formulates quality standards for goods and certifies products that meet them, allowing them to carry the ISI mark.
April 2025
What is meant by consumer protection?

Consumer protection means protecting consumers from unfair trade practices such as adulteration, overcharging and misleading advertisements, and providing them remedies through laws and consumer courts.

Name the consumer courts where complaints are filed.
District Commission (District Forum), State Commission and National Commission — set up under the Consumer Protection Act.

or: State two points of importance of consumer protection from the business's point of view.

(1) It builds goodwill and long-term customer loyalty.
(2) It is the social responsibility of business, and satisfied consumers mean larger sales.

Consumer Protection Act (1986). It gives consumers six rights and a simple, cheap and quick three-tier system of consumer courts to get replacement, refund or compensation.

(1) Adulteration of food and oil.

or: Why should a consumer look for the ISI mark on electrical goods?
The ISI mark shows the product meets the safety and quality standards of BIS, so it is safe to use and less likely to cause shocks or fire.

An air purifier advertised as removing 100% germs did not work for Priya; testing showed it had no such capacity. What malpractice is involved and which rights can she exercise?

Malpractice: misleading advertisement (false claim of quality).
Rights: right to be informed (she was given false information); right to seek redressal — she can file a complaint for refund or replacement and compensation in the District Commission; right to be heard.
October 2025
What precautions should consumers take while buying medicines?

(1) Check the expiry date and manufacturing date.
(2) Buy from a licensed chemist and insist on a cash memo.
(3) Check the MRP, batch number and that the seal is intact.
April 2025

or: How does the government protect consumers? Explain with three examples.

(1) Laws such as the Consumer Protection Act and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act punish unfair practices.
(2) Three-tier consumer courts give quick, cheap remedies.
(3) Standards and certification through BIS (ISI) and AGMARK; awareness campaigns like 'Jago Grahak Jago'.

(2) Giving legal aid and filing complaints on behalf of consumers.
(3) Comparative testing of products and publishing results; representing consumers in official bodies.

(1) Removal of defects in goods or deficiency in services.

la: Abhishek bought an ₹80,000 home theatre with one year's warranty. It stopped working and the dealer did not replace it. Which consumer court should he approach and why? Name the other courts with their jurisdiction. Which document must he have?

He should approach the District Commission (District Forum), because the value is ₹80,000 — within its limit.
Other courts (1986 Act): State Commission — ₹20 lakh to ₹1 crore; National Commission — above ₹1 crore. (2019 Act as revised: District up to ₹50 lakh, State ₹50 lakh–₹2 crore, National above ₹2 crore.)
He must have the cash memo (bill) and warranty card as proof of transaction.

Abhishek bought a ₹25 lakh machine to make room heaters; it was defective and the seller ignored his complaints. (a) Where can he file a complaint? (b) What remedies are available if the court is satisfied?

(a) Under the 1986 Act, the State Commission (₹20 lakh to ₹1 crore); under the 2019 Act as revised, the District Commission (up to ₹50 lakh).
(b) Removal of the defect; replacement of the machine; refund of the price; compensation for loss; stopping the unfair practice.

Explain the role of consumers, businessmen and government in consumer protection.

Consumers: self-help — be aware of rights, check quality marks, get bills, complain against cheating and form associations.
Businessmen: supply quality goods at fair prices, avoid malpractices, settle complaints; trade associations discipline members.
Government: pass and enforce laws, set up consumer courts and standards bodies (BIS), include consumer representatives in policy bodies, and run awareness programmes.
October 2022

October 2016
What is the purpose of (a) the Bureau of Indian Standards Act, 1986 (b) the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 (c) the Consumer Protection Act, 1986?

(a) BIS Act: to set quality standards for goods and certify conforming products with the ISI mark.
(b) Prevention of Food Adulteration Act: to prevent adulteration of food; it gives severe punishment, up to life imprisonment, and food inspectors can take samples.
(c) Consumer Protection Act: to protect consumers' six rights and give quick, cheap redressal through District, State and National consumer courts for goods and services.
April 2023
October 2017
Explain sale of spurious products, hoarding and black-marketing, and misleading advertisements.

Spurious products: worthless or fake goods sold as genuine, e.g. injections containing only water.
Hoarding and black-marketing: stocks of essential goods are held back to create scarcity, then sold secretly at higher prices.
Misleading advertisements: false claims about quality, use or price that deceive consumers into buying.
October 2021
Why is consumer protection required in India? Discuss.

(1) Many consumers are illiterate and ignorant of their rights.
(2) Consumers are unorganised and cannot fight big firms alone.
(3) Widespread malpractices — adulteration, short weights, spurious goods, hoarding.
(4) Misleading advertisements and a huge variety of products make choice hard.
(5) Services cannot be checked in advance. So laws, consumer courts and awareness are needed.
